title: Convex Hulls: From Mixtures To Boundaries
notes: Open with the mixture model from printed pages 243-244, but keep the language computational. A mixture is represented by coordinates, and a recipe is a vector of nonnegative weights whose sum is one. The first check on the slide is deliberately small: if the lambdas add to one and stay nonnegative, the target point is a feasible convex combination.

title: Convex Hull As Feasible Set
notes: Move from one recipe to the entire feasible region. The hull is the set of all recipes obtainable from the base points, so membership becomes an algorithmic question: can we find barycentric weights satisfying the nonnegativity and sum constraints? The inside and outside targets make the abstract definition inspectable.

title: From Polygon To Polytope
notes: Use this slide to shift the class from the familiar planar hull to the three-dimensional boundary structure used in the chapter. Vertices are input points, edges are shared by facets, and facets are maximal coplanar boundary polygons. The important computational idea is that the infinite solid is represented by a finite boundary complex.

title: Euler Controls Complexity
notes: Printed pages 244-245 use Euler's formula to show why three-dimensional hulls remain linear in size. Walk through the proof roadmap: interpret the boundary as a planar graph, count face-edge incidences, combine that with V minus E plus F equals two, and read off the edge and facet bounds.

title: Incremental Starting State
notes: The randomized algorithm starts only after four noncoplanar points are found. Emphasize the determinant test as the robust predicate hiding behind the word tetrahedron. If the determinant vanishes for every candidate fourth point, the problem has fallen back to a planar convex hull instance.

title: Visible Facets And Horizon
notes: Define visibility exactly enough for implementation. Each oriented facet carries a plane equation with the current hull on the nonpositive side. A new point sees precisely the facets with positive signed distance. The horizon is the cycle of edges separating visible facets from invisible facets.

title: Replacing The Visible Region
notes: Show the local edit that transforms CH of the old prefix into CH of the new prefix. Delete all visible facets, keep the invisible boundary, and connect the new point to the ordered horizon edges. The algorithm is efficient because it edits only the exposed patch rather than rebuilding the whole polytope.

title: DCEL Boundary State
notes: Connect the geometry to the data structure. The DCEL stores each edge twice, once for each incident facet, with twin, next, previous, origin, and face links. The outside counterclockwise convention matters because signed plane tests, horizon walks, and facet creation all depend on consistent orientation.

title: Conflict Lists
notes: Introduce the conflict graph as the work-ahead device that prevents testing every facet at every insertion. A future point is adjacent to exactly the current facets it can see. When that point is inserted, its neighbors in the graph are precisely the facets to delete.

title: Updating New Facets
notes: Explain the crucial update rule from printed pages 248-249. For a new facet built on a horizon edge, a future point can see it only if it could see at least one of the two old facets incident to that edge. Therefore the candidate set is the union of two old conflict lists, followed by fresh signed plane tests.

title: Coplanar Merge Failure Mode
notes: Pause on degeneracy rather than sweeping it under the carpet. If the new point lies in the supporting plane of an old facet, the triangular cones along that facet are not real new facets of the polytope; they must be merged into one maximal coplanar facet. This is also a reminder that the DCEL stores facets, not just triangles.

title: Random Order And Local Work
notes: Use the ledger to keep the randomized incremental state concrete. At each insertion we record whether the point is internal, how many facets are visible, how many horizon edges appear, how many new facets are created, and how many conflict arcs are touched. The notebook's sanity record gives a small reproducible instance with seven points and eight facets.

title: Backwards Analysis
notes: This is the core expectation argument from printed page 250. Instead of asking how many facets insertion creates, look backward from CH of the first r points and remove the last random vertex. The number of disappearing facets equals the degree of that vertex, and the average degree is bounded by Euler's edge bound.

title: Flaps And Running Time
notes: The O(n log n) bound needs more than the number of created facets because conflict updates scan candidate point sets. Flaps package each oriented horizon edge as a constant-size configuration. Configuration-space analysis then bounds the total size of all candidate lists over the random history.

title: Hulls Meet Half-Spaces
notes: Use the planar dual view from printed pages 253-254 as the bridge to half-space intersection. Upper hull edges become lower-envelope vertices after duality, and order reverses in a controlled way. The caveat is important: arbitrary half-plane intersection can be empty, while an ordinary Euclidean convex hull is always defined, so a fully general duality needs extra information such as an interior point.

title: Paraboloid Lift To Voronoi
notes: Close with the chapter's link back to Voronoi diagrams. Lifting a site to the unit paraboloid gives a tangent plane whose vertical gap at a query point is squared distance. The upper envelope of these planes projects to nearest-site cells, and by duality this is equivalent to a lower-hull computation, with the Delaunay graph appearing as the projected lower hull.
